Another key component of our model is the Meta NP (MNPS) model, which is a meta neural process model that is composed of a hyperdraw function and a neural process model. We evaluated our model on the specific task of emergent false news identification and obtained superior results when compared to the baseline models, particularly on visual-only and combined textual and visual

This paper formulates a conveyance equation with a time-periodic external force as a nonlinear evolution equation on a compact domain in one-dimensional space, and then establishes the key property of this equation's solution space being an isometric manifold. By determining the Lie algebra of symmetries within the solution space and its intersection with the space of conserved quantities, the paper is able to derive specific conservation laws for the equation's solutions. Additionally, we find the invariance of the solution space under the action of Lie group, and demonstrate that this invariance generates explicit solution patterns for the equation's solutions.

In a status refreshing system, updating information at optimal times can minimize costs, but the exact period is unknown and may depend on ongoing arrivals and service times. This study determines the optimal updating period on a discrete time basis for a specific type of queue, the Ber/G/1/1 queue, by analyzing the impact of arrival and service time on the system's behavior. A key finding is that the optimal updating period is in fact the minimum of several critical values related to the system's distribution functions, which can be a discrete fraction of the mean service time. Additionally, certain conditions on the distribution functions can guarantee that the optimal updating period is no more than half of the mean service time, which provides a practical way to determine a discrete time equivalent to the continuous time optimal period. A numerical analysis of different distributions shows that the optimal updating period can be a significant fraction of the mean service time, which can lead to a substantial reduction in updating costs.

This work delves into Yang-Baxter operators and their underlying degree n tuples, which are essentially combinations of n-1 matrices that satisfy a specific equation. We then focus on set-theoretic solutions of this equation and explore their properties. By applying a specific transformation to these solutions, we derive quasi-bialgebras and demonstrate that the original solutions are closely linked to the derived quasi-bialgebras. We also establish that the degree n tuple of a set-theoretic solution can be represented as a direct sum of the identity matrix and other matrices, which are part of the same solution. This direct sum essentially conveys the information contained in the original solution and can be used to develop new solutions. We further demonstrate that the algebra and coalgebra structures associated with a set-theoretic solution are isomorphic and that the multiplication and comultiplication operators associated with the solution are bijective. We then introduce the concept of a generic solution of the Yang-Baxter equation and explore its underlying degree n tuple, which is comprised of the identity matrix and other matrices that satisfy specific equations. We establish that a generic solution can be represented as a direct sum of the identity matrix and other matrices, which are part of the same solution. This direct sum essentially conveys the information contained in the original solution and can be used to develop new solutions. We further demonstrate that the algebra and coalgebra structures associated with a set-theoretic solution are isomorphic and that the multiplication and comultiplication operators associated

A new construction method for odd-order Golay complementary pairs in four dimensions is proposed, based on a modified form of a quartic polynomial. Using a concept similar to the one used in a previous paper by K. Ayra and M. Kumar, the constructed pairs can be extended to Golay complementary sets in four dimensions. The number of elements in these sets is given by $N = (n^2 - 1)(n^2 - \epsilon)$. $\epsilon$ is used to distinguish between sets of Golay complementary quadruples and octuples in four dimensions. The value of $\epsilon$ is 1 for quadruple sets and 9 for octuple sets. A specific set in four dimensions with $N = 255$ has been found using this construction method. It remains unknown whether the largest size of a Golay complementary set in four dimensions is 255. Therefore, this paper also proposes a method for forming Golay complementary sets in $p$ dimensions, using a particular set of functions.

Quantum tunneling of spin states at the atomic level in semiconductors is heavily dependent on interaction between adjacent valleys within the same atom. Although this interaction is highly influential, it remains somewhat mysterious due to the difficulty in experimentally measuring these effects directly. Employing advanced theoretical models and experimental data from silicon-29, we have developed a method to measure this interaction at the atomic scale and found that it results in the splitting of spin states. Furthermore, by adjusting the spin of a nearest neighbor electron, we were able to induce a significant transfer of spin states in a distant silicon atom, with a rate that could be as high as 100 MHz. This breakthrough also enables the creation of robust, quantum entanglement between two silicon atoms, with a fidelity of over 99.9%.

In our research, we employ graph neural networks to analyze the temporal evolution of complex dynamic systems. We achieve this by treating system time series data as numerical representations, transforming temporal sequences into discrete temporal neural network models, and using graph neural networks to capture the temporal dynamics and underlying structure. We significantly improve the existing method of manual feature engineering by automating the process, which results in more accurate predictions and a better understanding of the complex system's temporal evolution and internal structure. We validate our approach through experiments involving a social impact network and solar network data.

Levine-Morey's formula for computing $\pi_*(D_{k+n})$ relies on the value of $d_{k+n}$, which represents the number of ways to divide $k+n$ into pairs of positive integers. To expand upon this, we derive closed-form expressions for $d_n$ by reinterpreting the problem within combinatorial frameworks, ultimately providing recursive formulas and specific values for $d_n$. These results, in turn, inform a general conjecture regarding the behavior of $d_n$ in relation to homology theories associated with simplicial sets.

A recent advancement in medical research known as the AutoContext framework has shown significant potential in creating advanced lesion detection tools. However, its limitation in handling complex lesions with indistinct boundaries poses a substantial challenge. To overcome this constraint, a new method has been devised by combining the AutoContext framework with a progressive variant of the Variational AutoEncoder, where a second model is used to accurately identify and outline lesions that were previously undetected. Nevertheless, existing variants of this progressive method are restricted to consecutive scale levels, which means they are incapable of modeling relationships between lesions across different scales. To address this shortfall, a new progressive Adversarial Variational AutoEncoder has been proposed, where a layer-based encoding scheme is used, where each encoding layer is responsible for identifying lesions at a specific scale level. Furthermore, a novel experiment has been devised to evaluate the performance of this proposed method, where a dataset containing cerebral lesions from multiple scale levels is used, and the results show that this method outperforms the existing state-of-the-art technique, the AutoContext framework, and other progressive methods.

We investigate the robustness of quantum nonlocality for unextendible product bases (UPBs) in multipartite systems, focusing on scenarios where different parties possess mutually independent sets of states. Our analysis reveals that the quantum nonlocality of UPBs exhibits distinct behavior based on the number of systems each party controls. In particular, in a tripartite scenario, we found that the minimal number of entangled pairs required to approximate an UPB representation exceeds the number of local maximally entangled states by two, indicating a robust nonlocal effect that can withstand contamination up to $\frac{7}{5}$, which is achieved by modifying a previous UPB of size $6 \times 6 \times 4$ using quantum nonlocality of multi-qurtets. Furthermore, we established that in a system with four or more parties, the minimal number of entangled pairs needed to approximate an UPB representation can be as low as two, with respect to certain UPB of size $d^3$, which can be viewed as a extension of Duan's argument to multipartite scenarios.

The speed at which computers exchange data can significantly impact the coordination of automated telescopes in large-scale astronomical surveys. Our study evaluates the total secure coordination time it takes for two telescopes to exchange data, a process deemed critical to avoiding data conflicts that would render observations useless. We measured this coordination time in a simulated environment based on the SDSS-V design, with factors including message priority, packet loss rate, and the number of simultaneous connections being tested. Our results indicate that even under perfect conditions, there is a non-zero risk of coordination failure. We also found that increasing the number of simultaneous connections can significantly decrease the average and maximum secure coordination times, while prioritizing data exchanges has a negative impact on total secure coordination times. Furthermore, in an ideal scenario, failing to implement data verification would result in complete coordination failure within 24 hours. Additionally, we found that the effects of packet loss on secure coordination times are minimal, but the choice of encryption method does have an impact, with some methods increasing the risk of failure by up to five times.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformations and matching. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties for programmers who are not experts in graph theory, due to the required explicit handling of graph structures. To overcome these challenges, we enhanced the GP 2 compiler with node ordering optimization, reducing graph traversal inefficiencies and making-programmer tasks more manageable. Additionally, we incorporated a wrapper feature that facilitates seamless integration with external tools, such as model checkers and type checkers. These improvements transform the GP 2 compiler into a more versatile and user-friendly development environment, suitable for a broader range of programmers.

Deep Neural Networks have been the go-to method for image classification using local invariant features. However, the success of these networks remains largely dependent on the quality of handcrafted convolutional neural network features used during training. In contrast, the proposed Comparative Convolutional Neural Network extracts relevant visual information automatically through comparative learning. This occurs during a two-stage process where the network learns to compare local descriptors in two sets - one set is derived from random sampling of the dataset, while the other is obtained through the comparison of descriptors in the training dataset. Upon further analysis, it becomes apparent that comparative convolutional neural networks possess characteristics similar to traditional extraction methods including invariant manifolds, dimensional reduction, and pattern discovery. We argue that the behavior of comparative convolutional neural networks can be understood through the lens of non-linear dimensionality reduction, supported by empirical evidence demonstrating the efficacy of this approach. In line with these findings, we propose a novel comparative convolutional neural network structure that leverages multi-linear dimensionality reduction to enhance performance. Experimental results validate our approach, yielding improvements over the baseline model on multiple datasets.

We have derived an infinitely diverse series of infinite graphs whose connection groups are linked to the action of twisted wreath groups on a normal star diagram. This achievement comes from a unique association between twisted wreath groups and certain types of graph automorphism groups. As a result, we can create an infinite range of infinite graphs with distinct properties by applying various twisted wreath groups to a regular star diagram.

Working with categorical data for feature selection and model sparsity becomes increasingly difficult as the number of variables grows, as it requires handling polynomial interactions between nominal features. The challenge lies in the high dimensionalality of such data, which exceeds the sample size and poses a substantial obstacle to conventional methods. Although recent techniques like the Group Lasso and its extensions can handle groupings of variables, they may struggle with categorical data due to its inherent non-linearity. In contrast, our enhanced Group Lasso approach can efficiently handle a large number of nominal variables with no need for pseudo-observations, achieving this through a combination of mutual information and an efficient Newton-Raphson solver. We evaluate this method on several real-world datasets, finding it outperforms existing techniques and is particularly effective at selecting relevant features from high-dimensional datasets.

Recent advances in large language models have shown a high dependence on pre-trained models with limited domain expertise and extensive training data. Despite this, these models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to learn general knowledge structures from vast amounts of unstructured text. Based on this observation, our approach takes a different methodology where the primary source of knowledge is a highly-trained language model. We integrate this model with a set of rules that enable the efficient creation of knowledge graphs, ultimately producing a model that can generate novel statements of fact. We achieve this through the development of specific tools that transform natural language sentences into directed graphs, using the Mynamed tool to leverage named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging. Furthermore, we introduce a custom graph matcher called G-LoWa, built using Marmalade, a graph manipulation language. G-LoWa is particularly useful for identifying potential relationships between entities across a knowledge graph. We also introduce a new method for creating bi-directional entity relationships within a graph. We evaluated our approach against a set of existing knowledge graphs and found that our method produces results that are highly accurate when compared to human annotations.

This study examines a nonlocal dispersion model, investigates its properties through mathematical and numerical analyses, and explores how it relates to established local transport equations. We demonstrate that by applying suitable nonlocal kernels, our model aligns with both the fractional derivative approach and traditional local transport equations. Further, we utilize explicit numerical schemes to analyze the model's behavior in different contexts. The study reveals that the model's solution can exhibit both positive and negative values, which may seem inconsistent with standard local transport equations. However, we demonstrate that this behavior is a consequence of the model's definition and can be understood by examining the model's initial conditions. The article also discusses the challenge of developing numerical methods for the fractional Cattaneo model, particularly due to the restriction imposed by Gibbs' phenomenon on acceptable approximations. Ultimately, we evaluate the model's behavior under various fractional order conditions and provide discrete consistency criteria for numerical schemes. The article concludes with a discussion on the significance of fractional order $\alpha$ in the context of fractional order fractional Cattaneo model.

When photographing scenes, the position of objects is influenced by gravity, with a consistent orientation in mind's eye. This intuitive concept is difficult to quantify, but it is reflected in photos that reflect this bias. The scope of this research is to limit the possibilities of combining partial photos to those aligned with this perceived orientation. A specific gravitational axis is determined by identifying photos that naturally point in this direction. Only combinations of photos that naturally point towards this axis are considered, significantly reducing the number of potential combinations. This approach ensures coherence and allows for more realistic projections of the combined photos. The method was tested with artificial data and applied to combining partial photos of real scenes from various sources.

In 1987, Gelbart and Gelfand proved that certain Eisenstein series for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ have nontrivial completions of algebraic forms, and this result was further expanded upon by Ginzburg in 2002. Building on the work of Ginzburg, we demonstrate that a specific subset of these Eisenstein series completes to algebraic forms of degree six for $n=4$, and our method employs a combination of sieve formulas and partial sums of Whittaker functions. Additionally, our approach enables us to derive nontrivial bounds for the zeros of these Eisenstein series.

Our research involves developing a cutting-edge biophysical computational model of the brain, specifically focusing on a region critical to movement control known as the subthalamic nucleus (STN). This project leverages advanced computing technologies and access to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of the marmoset primate brain to create a highly detailed, species-specific simulation environment. By combining sophisticated neurobiological processes and a comprehensive neurotransmitter system, our model aims to provide valuable insights into abnormal Parkinson's disease brain function. Furthermore, it has the capability to be used in various scenarios, including the evaluation of surgical interventions and the optimization of deep brain stimulation techniques.

The increasing adoption of electric vehicles and autonomous navigation relies heavily on high-definition maps that are created through real-world sensor data, yet these maps can be marred by aliasing artifacts caused by the rendering of non-smooth lines. While traditional aliasing removal techniques are computationally expensive and unsuitable for real-time applications, our novel framework leverages spatial awareness and prioritization to efficiently eliminate aliasing at line junctions, yielding a 50ms rendering time and outperforming existing methods by 5-10x.

Our team used the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope to conduct spatially integrated gas observations of extremely luminous infrared galaxies within the GOALS sample at low redshifts. We shared our preliminary findings for nine objects at U/LIRGs, focusing on star-forming rates, gas masses, and outflow properties. A high correlation was observed between star-forming rates and gas masses, and the majority of these galaxies exhibited signs of gas outflows. However, we discovered that gas outflows were prevalent even in low-luminosity IRGs, contradicting previous theories suggesting outflows only develop in powerful ULIRGs.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to divide a given domain into segments. However, this approach can lead to an excessive number of nodes being required for a specific interpolation accuracy, which in turn causes issues with the potential instability and low efficiency of the algorithm. To address these challenges, a novel algorithm is proposed that employs a transcendental interpolation function independent of the partitioning of the domain. The proposed interpolation function takes the form of a combination of Gaussian functions, which are known for their global convergence properties. The algorithm is based on the use of piecewise piecewise linear or quadratic functions to approximate the weights of the Gaussian function combination, which reduces the computational complexity. The proposed algorithm is proven to preserve the form of linear, quadratic, and cubic functions, and has a global convergence order of $min(2r,r+1)$ for the case of $r$-times differentiable functions. Notably, this algorithm is the first example of an interpolation algorithm that preserves the form of quadratic functions, and it outperforms the classic algorithm based on Gaussian processes in terms of efficiency and accuracy.

Cloud categorization holds significant significance in understanding the formation of clouds, which directly impacts weather forecasting. However, accurately identifying clouds through visual means is challenging and tends to yield inconsistent results even among trained meteorologists. This difficulty highlights the need for a semi-accurate cloud database that can facilitate advancements in cloud analysis and ultimately aid in weather prediction. In an effort to address this issue, researchers have introduced the use of super-resolution techniques in cloud databases. Yet, a considerable disparity persists between artificially generated high-resolution images and real-world images characterized by limited resolution. The primary concern lies not with the technical capability but with the scarcity of suitable data. To address this limitation, researchers have explored the feasibility of using data enhancement methods that mimic real-world transformations. The introduction of the WeatherCateg dataset represents a breakthrough in multi-label cloud classification. Comprising 10 distinct classes and involving 10,000 high-resolution images, this dataset poses a formidable challenge for convolutional neural networks. To enhance the dataset's classification robustness, a novel data augmentation strategy has been developed, incorporating real-world transfer learning and disparate transformation techniques. The evaluation of this dataset reveals that the application of state-of-the-art CNNs yields promising results, with an average accuracy of 87.1% on the test set. Notably, a custom-designed network emerged as the top performer, achieving a remarkable 93.8% accuracy on the test set.

A Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network named DPCRN is introduced in this paper for independent component analysis in a noiser. Research has shown the effectiveness of Dual-Path networks in both convolutional and recurrent setups. However, combining these architectures using a shared representation can lead to overfitting due to increased parameters. To address this issue, DPCRN uses two separate dual-path networks: one for the temporal and one for the frequency domain. Furthermore, a comparison is made with other popular ICA methods including Independent Component Analysis, Deep Neural Network, and Convolution Recurrent Network. Evaluations were conducted on the TIMIT dataset using the Noisy-TIMIT dataset as noise and DPCRN was found to perform better than these methods with an average RFR of 0.9346.

A new analysis of the impact of fifth-dimensional gravity and heavy neutrinos on the structure of dark matter has been performed, applying the principles of screening that prevent over-cosmological effects.  The researchers developed a set of non-linear equations governing the behavior of dark matter halos in a variety of $f(R)$ gravity models with neutrino effects.  By relying on the properties of halos at their turn-around points, an assessment was made of the combined influence of these cosmological systems on the radial distribution of matter within halos.  The role of screening was examined through a series of ideal cosmological simulations.  The findings of this study indicate that even non-linear effects can be understood through a simple, linear superposition of the impacts of $f(R)$ gravity and heavy neutrinos on the turn-around radii of dark matter halos.

Recently introduced multi-fluid simulations converge to the correct solution for atmospheric convection when coupled with a limited number of interacting fluid layers. We propose a two-fluid simulation approach by dividing the atmosphere into two separate entities: air with gas-phase water vapor and cloud water droplets or ice particles. The paper demonstrates the technique using a simple Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard cell model, with an emphasis on the importance of dynamic coupling between the two fluid layers. The approach is then validated against traditional single-fluid simulations, and the results show that multi-fluid simulations yield more accurate temperature gradient calculations due to the prevention of excessive heat transfer between distinct fluid layers. The paper also explores potential applications of the two-fluid approach to modeling atmospheric convection using large-eddy simulation.

Any interaction between two isolated particles of comparable mass, such as photons, must first meet specific criteria to achieve a highly entangled state through various means such as Jaynes-Cummings interactions. Unfortunately, most approaches devised so far to accomplish this entanglement fall short of genuinely connecting the particles. A new method has been developed that employs a combination of beam splitters and not-all-to-all linear optical components to successfully generate a highly entangled state from uncorrelated input photons. Interestingly, this technique works equally well for photons of different frequencies. Nonetheless, using this method in real-world applications may be impeded by the phenomenon of photon hopping, which causes the entanglement to decay over time. Nonetheless, researchers believe that this newly devised method will have far-reaching implications for the study of Jaynes-Cummings models and may also be adapted for use with other types of entangling interactions.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although it operates within a 3.8 Tesla magnetic field, making the tracking of particles complex, a thorough understanding of the particle path is crucial. However, the detector's performance is hampered by the cooling of the closest layer of the detector to -80 degrees Celsius, which induces an energy gradient across its surface. As a result, the development of an electrical gradient in the order of a few millivolts has been observed, posing a significant challenge to the reconstruction of the in-plane edge pixels. To mitigate this issue, the charge collection pattern of the edge pixels is re-examined by adjusting the shape-fit function to a more complex form, thereby yielding a notable improvement in the edge pixel's hit efficiency.

A novel method using Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral decomposition has been successfully applied to compute the mass spectrum of the scalar SU(2) glueball on the lattice. This approach yields a spectral sum rule that is invariant under gauge transformations and ensures the positivity of the spectral function, which in turn guarantees the reality of the mass spectrum for the ground state. Our findings, supported by four different types of spectral functions, confirm the previously reported mass value of approximately 1.66 GeV for the scalar SU(2) glueball. This method can be extended to study other hadron spectra.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, accurately determining the sentiment expressed in individual tweets becomes
crucial. Many studies have explored various techniques, including the use of supervised
machine learning models, to better understand and predict the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. In this study, we experiment with a simple yet effective supervised
approach using a single neural network model, specifically a Long Short-Term Memory
(LSTM) network, to predict the sentiment expressed in individual tweets. We evaluated
this approach using a subset of the Sentiment400 dataset, containing 20000 randomly
selected tweets, and achieved significant improvements over existing baseline models.

A nonlinear interaction between an external massless field and a black hole can result in a more complex metric that may not be described by a linear response theory. We examined the interaction of a massless scalar field with a nonlinear charged anti-de Sitter black hole to demonstrate how it produces a shadow ring with an irregular edge, mimicking an effect observed in general relativity. By analyzing the transition from a low-energy, linear response regime to a higher-energy, non-linear regime, we discovered that the shadow's irregular edge behavior could provide insights into the black hole's charge in certain environments.

Reversing the process of state preparation in a quantum system of two components, either bosonic particles or a two-state system of spin-1/2 particles, yields a non-standard version of their entanglement. We refer to this altered entanglement as GLE for short. Obtaining the tomogram of this modified entanglement state is not straightforward and typically involves a lengthy calculation. In our research, we identify specific transformations of the Wigner function that allow us to derive the tomogram of the Gaussian modified-entanglement (GLE) state through a simple transformation of the standard Gaussian-entanglement state's tomogram. We further demonstrate that in certain situations, specifically when the standard and GLE states coexist, the difference in their tomograms can indicate the onset of synchronization. Our approach also facilitates the comparison of standard and GLE states across various angles and in relation to specific transformations.

Building a conversational interface for a role-defined conversation requires not only an understanding of the overall structure but also specific information related to that structure. Achieving this involves not only comprehension but also the ability to generate coherent and contextually relevant text. While current language models excel at both individual tasks, they still fall short in combination. Nonetheless, recent advancements in language models have demonstrated potential in expanding our understanding of what is possible with human language. In this work, we explore the application of large language models to a role-defined conversation scenario. To facilitate conversation, we developed a set of rules that govern not only the overall conversation thread but also individual utterances. Grounding these rules in semantics rather than syntax enables us to leverage the predictive capabilities of large language models. In our implementation, we integrated multiple T5 models to create a system that not only matches our pre-defined conversation structure but also conveys the intended meaning. Although our results show that such a system can achieve near-human performance, there is still room for improvement in generating more natural and varied language. Nonetheless, our findings suggest that role-defined conversations can be effectively constructed using large language models and may have broader implications for language generation.

Precision agriculture's key component is the analysis of pest control methods using mathematical models, specifically optimal control theory and variational analysis. A strong approach is a powerful tool for studying optimal control problems involving differential equations, closely tied to the study of agricultural management problems. In the context of controlling plant diseases, a strong approach can provide valuable insights, such as identifying the minimum rate at which treatments should be applied to minimize the economic impact of disease at a given time. However, in practice, there are limitations to increasing treatment rates, which can be factored into the analysis. This paper demonstrates the application of a strong approach to the management of strawberry fungal disease in California, identifying the optimal application schedule for fungicides in Santa Cruz and Watsonville based on weather conditions and the disease's progression. The analysis shows that in certain weather conditions, the disease can spread exponentially, affecting the effectiveness of control methods. The findings also indicate that in some situations, the optimal control strategy can reduce the economic impact of disease by 50%. The research highlights the importance of collaborating with farmers and agricultural scientists to interpret the results in a practical context and informs the development of more complex management models that can handle multiple crop growth stages and exogenous variables.

As 360-degree virtual travel videos gain popularity, providing an immersive viewing experience with minimal technical setup, a new method of captioning is emerging to make travel planning accessible to visually impaired tourists.  We propose an innovative AI system that uses a unique dataset consisting of 360-degree captions and corresponding image descriptions.  Our data-driven analysis indicates that current state-of-the-art visual captioning models struggle to accurately predict captions from a first-person perspective.  To address this challenge, we've developed a 360-degree captioning model that learns to forecast entire paragraph captions by processing a limited viewport of the 360-degree video.  Our experiments demonstrate substantial gains in accuracy compared to baseline models, indicating that forecasted captions can be highly reliable.  Interestingly, our findings suggest that only a limited subset of necessary words is consistently identified across multiple viewport predictions, paving the way for efficient, data-driven travel planning applications.  We're excited to share our dataset, which comprises over 800 thousand word tokens, and our model's code to facilitate further advancements in 360-degree captioning.

Tensor network methods have commonly been used to compute the time evolution of quantum many-body systems and thermal equilibrium by employing approximations such as the iTPA algorithm. These algorithms typically involve constructing a TN representation of the time-evolved or thermal state of a system, which may not accurately capture its original properties. In contrast, our work presents a novel tensor network representation that is precisely local in both space and time for any quantum system's thermal state or time-evolved state. We demonstrate the benefits of this representation by showing an expansion algorithm for arbitrary TN representations that results in the precisely local tensor network representation. We also derive an approximate contraction algorithm for the precisely local tensor network representation, which serves as a variant of the iTPA algorithm and yields a similar tensor network representation that can be efficiently contracted. Notably, this approximation outperforms the iTPA algorithm by a factor of over ten in terms of contraction time for a specific example system.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse group of ODEs on a linear timescale, building on a similar approach introduced in [AR20]. Our work is guided by the principle that when the rapid component of the solution meets certain criteria, the behavior of the system is determined by a simplified, reduced system. In contrast to [AR20], our approach focuses on a broader category of systems, including those with asymptotically stable or neutrally stable critical layers, as well as systems exhibiting non-transverse intersections. We demonstrate that a scale-oriented approximation, even if restricted to a particular efficacy, can yield a valid and accurate approximation of the solution over an extended timescale. This is illustrated through specific examples, including a system with a stable focal point and a system representing a critically stable plane.

In this research, we establish a nonisotropic $p$-capacity inequality that mirrors the isoperimetric inequality. As a result, we derive a nonisotropic Minkowski inequality. Our approach to proving the nonisotropic $p$-capacity inequality involves manipulating a rearrangement inequality specific to isoperimetric inequalities. We then leverage this inequality, along with a quantitative version of a symmetry result, to demonstrate the Minkowski inequality. A key aspect of our proof, the quantitative symmetry result can be derived from the nonisotropic $p$-capacity inequality itself.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves comparing the motion of two test masses as they orbit the Earth, influenced by gravitational forces. Mass discrimination is achieved through differences in the frequencies of two types of oscillations between the test masses and their support structure. This experiment aims to induce a specific relative motion between the masses in an attempt to detect a predicted difference, which results from various non-gravitational interactions. However, the success of this test depends on the duration of specific intense solar flares known as SOLAR FLARES, or simply GLITCHES, which cause sudden and temporary disruptions in the data. We have developed a statistical method to identify potential glitches in the data and assess their impact on the test of the weak equivalence principle. Using this approach, we have analyzed the effects of real-time data and determined that the Microscope space test will exceed its desired sensitivity to reference frequency fluctuations caused by solar flares, occurring at least once per year, assuming the test continues for two years.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy is utilized to create precise nanoscale gradients of superhydrophobicity along with various surface chemistry changes across specific lengths. The ability of colloidal particles to move dynamically in response to these gradients, which both attract and repel water, is studied through a combination of experimental observations and computational simulations. The observed particle behavior is explained by a simplified model that takes into account the dynamic interaction between particles and changing surface free energy conditions and is further validated through simulations of particle interactions within three-dimensional environments.

The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, where we also examine 2-hops covers for specific graphs and show the general k-hops cover problem is NP-complete.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby changing the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\chi^2=1$ times the power variation, with a specific value of two times the mean squared deviation. This increased uncertainty is expected to be observable in LHCb's predicted outputs, with shifts of up to 20 ns in the mean lifetime and 5 GeV in the mass of heavy mesons.

As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior on a toral annulus shifts from transient to recurrent. We have found that on a two-dimensional toral annulus, the exact critical density for this transition is the number of sites in the largest tree component within the annulus.

Researchers are focusing on the intersection of photonics and magnetism to achieve very high, orientation-dependent effects that can't be attributed to either field alone. This work centers on a unique magnetophotonic surface lattice with deeply interlinked ensembles of nanowires, presented from an aerial perspective. When this structure is exposed to polarized light, it exhibits an extraordinary capacity for light localization, and remarkable shifts in photon momentum can occur under magnetic fields. This phenomenon leads to an extraordinary interaction between light and the external magnetic field, resulting in a massive change in the lattice's spatial periodicity in a direction determined by the angle between two key components. As a result, the lattice can switch between supporting two distinct types of localized light states. This unique characteristics are also shown to cause a significant increase in the lattice's susceptibility to optical nonlinear effects by approximately two to three orders of magnitude, making it possible to observe this orientation-dependent phenomenon even at relatively low magnetic fields without the need for precise orientation control.

Knowledge acquisition in models like linear regression and tree-based methods is inherently straightforward due to their transparent nature. Nonetheless, when we deal with complex machine learning models such as random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks, it becomes difficult to obtain their intermediate decision-making processes. This paper seeks to address this challenge by introducing a novel, zero-shot knowledge transfer framework from a black-box perspective. We designed a decision-based proxy model that can effectively interpret the complex model's decision-making processes by matching their risk profiles. We leveraged this proxy model to develop a knowledge transfer technique capable of adapting to any target model without the need for additional training. We assessed our framework's performance on multiple datasets, demonstrating a notable increase in predictive accuracy when compared to the original model.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. For certain modules, such as those representing linear representations of a group, this construct is well-defined and can be visualized through a diagram known as a fusion tree. Given a set of irreducible submodules of a module, along with their fusion rules, we can determine other submodules of the module. These submodules may not be irreducible and could potentially form a lattice that is not a set of distinct, non-overlapping lines. To avoid confusion, terms like simple, irreducible, and fundamental are used correctly in this context. If a module contains a submodule that is not irreducible, it is considered fundamental. To build its lattice, we can use a step-by-step procedure that begins with its top and bottom elements and fills in the gaps between them.

A strong geodetic set in a graph connects specific nodes to all other nodes in the shortest path. Identifying all strong geodetic sets in a graph is a highly complex problem, as demonstrated by G. M. Kamel and V. Kumar in 1989. We have discovered that determining a single strong geodetic set is NP-hard. We can solve this set-finding problem efficiently for some graph subtypes, such as trees, by applying a greedy algorithm. However, as the size of the tree increases, its asymptotic complexity becomes linear. We have also established that identifying a single strong geodetic set is doable in polynomial time for certain types of trees, such as binary trees and caterpillar trees. Conversely, we have shown that the general case of tree graph sets is NP-hard. We have developed a heuristic algorithm to solve the strong geodetic set-finding problem efficiently, as indicated by its asymptotic complexity of O(n.5^2), although we were unable to establish a guaranteed performance limit for this algorithm.

We have designed a novel concept for efficient imitation learning algorithms that can effectively utilize subpar training data to create policies surpassing the original behavior. Unlike traditional imitation learning methods which minimize the discrepancy between the training data and the desired policy, our approach involves training a model that perfectly mimics a high-quality policy utilizing a smaller, inferior dataset. The key challenge lies in determining an appropriate lower bound for the quality of the training data. We have developed a quantitative measure to address this issue. Furthermore, our approach is theoretically proven to yield near-optimal performance when the training data meets this quality standard. Moreover, we have tested our approach across multiple mimicry learning scenarios involving complex tasks, and the results demonstrate its efficacy.

Intelligent robots require high-quality training data to excel in complex tasks like object manipulation, but would benefit from human feedback in the form of observations about their actions. The issue lies in obtaining reliable, high-quality co-observations (action-outcome pairs with accompanying human annotations) due to the difficulty of simultaneously tracking both a robot's actions and resulting outcomes. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel co-observation learning framework that leverages unlabelled action-outcome data and incorporates human feedback in the form of simple comparisons between intended actions and actual outcomes. The key components of our approach are the introduction of a comparison-based annotation interface that human instructors find manageable, and a learning algorithm capable of processing this type of annotation. The benefits of this co-observation learning framework are validated through the implementation of a challenging reaching task, and the resulting policy is found to generalize effectively to novel objects and environments. The success of our approach is attributed to the generation of robust co-observation data, and the inclusion of human-in-the-loop feedback that significantly surpasses the performance of models trained via isolationist self-supervision.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an integer code distance, 
which is a crucial element for the efficient decoding of pulse-position modulation 
codes, particularly those based on additive-white Gaussian noise. We also derive a 
direct formula and an algorithm to calculate the average code distance of partial-parallel-continuous-phase-alignment-code (PAC) codes.

Using reinforcement learning post neural machine translation can improve performance, but it's challenging due to the large number of possible actions. We address this by designing two efficient frameworks to reduce computation and accelerate learning in both batch and mini-batch settings. In the first framework, we group similar words together based on their semantic and syntactic properties, then use a non-linear clustering algorithm to create a hierarchical structure of actions. This results in a more manageable action space with significant computational benefits and improved performance. In the second framework, we reduce actions by identifying words that are less translationally challenging and more semantically rich. We evaluate these frameworks on low-resource neural machine translation tasks with limited parallel data and find they outperform existing methods.

A novel method is introduced that enables a robot to adjust its camera and calculate the end-effector's position using only verbal feedback from a human instructor. A key innovation is the development of an innovative algorithm called K-FE, which leverages kernel-based methods to classify unknown object points by analyzing the distribution of previously marked data points. Another significant contribution is the introduction of two optimization techniques, projected gradient descent and batch optimization, for accurately estimating the end-effector's position using a nonlinear equation based on the marks provided by the human instructor. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of simulated experiments, as well as a practical experiment in which a robot is instructed to take pictures of various objects using a camera attached to the end-effector, with the goal of estimating the end-effector's position.

Quantum financial markets (QFM) are emerging as key areas for quantum applications, offering improved performance in specific tasks over their classical counterparts. Researchers are now exploring the potential of QFM to surpass random walk performance in specific scenarios. In this study, we introduce the quantum financial system-area (QFS-area) as a measure of market efficiency and correlate it with changes in market conditions. We discover that QFS-area is maximized when the interest rate of risk-free assets is equal to the average return of the stock, consistent with the concept that the highest level of market efficiency occurs when all assets are fully utilized. Additionally, QFS-area is affected by the number of trading steps and varies accordingly. It is interesting to note that, unlike classical random walk, the quantum walk does not converge to a random distribution over time.

The rise of partisan polarization in the United States can be inferred by analyzing the dividing influence of political online engagement on the consumption of news. To explore this phenomenon, a new dataset of 25 million users consuming online news over 5 years is presented. It reveals that users with high political scores in search results tend to exhibit increased polarization when consuming news, according to metrics such as click-through rates, engagement levels with websites, and platform-specific indicators. Additionally, the research discovers that the impact of political orientation on news consumption varies depending on the platform used, while polarization is found to be more prevalent among men than women and among men who are married than those who are single. Furthermore, it is observed that polarization decreases with increasing age and has different effects on different income groups.

We examine the word problem of R. Thompson's group V using a combinatorial approach, and derive a complex problem, related to the space of R. Thompson's group V, that remains unsolved for almost all finite generators of V. This problem has connections to combinatorial problems in various subshifts of finite type. By contrast, we show that the word problem of V is solvable in a straightforward manner for some special finite generator configurations. This word problem of V has been previously studied by Bootts, who established that it is a non-context-free problem for a particular set of generators. Our research confirms that it is a context-sensitive but Turing-complete problem for most finite generators of V, and it remains an open question whether it could be a recursively enumerable but not Turing-complete problem for some generators.

To grasp the behavior of open quantum systems under periodic disturbances, researchers typically resort to quasi-adiabatic theories that focus on equilibrium scenarios. In contrast, this study delves into the realm of non-equilibrium steady states in a periodically driven two-state system. Both experimental and theoretical findings on a freely evolving quantum system, represented by rubidium atoms employing a laser-driven transition between two states, revealed similar patterns when analyzed through a theoretical approach involving time-series correlations. This approach involves non-equilibrium steady states and identifies key differences between driven systems and their isolated, adiabatically driven counterparts. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that the experimental data can be accurately replicated using a theoretical model that accounts for non-equilibrium steady states, and identifies the unique spectral signatures that distinguish these states from their equilibrium counterparts in the spectrum of the correlation function.

We explore how the biharmonic operators on hypersurfaces in Euclidean space can be defined using repetitive operators by examining biharmonic hypersurfaces with the repeated Ricci operator. We discover that most common repetitive hypersurfaces are actually minimal. We then establish the conditions under which a hypersurface will be a linear combination of two parallel vector fields. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a hypersurface meeting these conditions must be a linear combination of two parallel vector fields if its curvature is constant. We also prove that if a hypersurface has a constant curvature and is a linear combination of two parallel vector fields, then its curvature must be zero.

A number set can be considered p/q-identifiable if the fraction p/q allows for the determination of individual nonresidue values within the set to the congruity of p-th power. Our research seeks to identify the possible instances of 1/q-identifiability in a random distribution of quadratic nonresidues, with specific attention to 5-identifiability in a random distribution of quadratic nonresidues modulo a prime number.

The axion's role in resolving the strong CP problem makes it an extremely refined physical concept. Nonetheless, we'll be exploring a more rudimentary, shadowy substance made up of axion-like particles that could violate CP symmetry, potentially neutrino non-zero masses, and possibly explain cosmological anomalies. By combining the effects of a CP-violating axion-like substance on neutrino oscillations, we found that the existence of a very light axion with a very large non-zero volume could, at a 2$\sigma$ confidence level, meet the conditions for the neutrino mass matrix to be positive definite. Furthermore, this substance could also be responsible for the sinusoidal modulation in the electron flux observed in the DAMPE dataset, and we found that the parameters for this dataset fall within the allowed 2$\sigma$ confidence level. All the model's allowed parameter combinations can be probed by the SHI experiments at the SNS user facility, and the theory can be tested with the CHET experiment at the CHIC facility, both located in Canada, and the HICOSM experiment at the HL-LHC in CERN, Switzerland.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST conducted a total of six observing campaigns over a specific time frame, totaling 110 hours of data collection. This report focuses on the results from four $K$2 plates that were used to gather information on various targets, including exoplanets, binary stars, and pulsars. A total of 1887 transits of 687 targets were detected with high confidence, representing a 27% increase in the known number of targets showing transit phenomena. Among these targets, 21 candidates were identified as being associated with exoplanets, and 16 of these were confirmed through additional research. Additionally, 12 targets exhibiting pulsational behavior were identified, and 5 targets showing eclipse phenomena were found, with 3 of these being associated with the pulsating star K2-139.

In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. A comprehensive visual analysis must account for both elements. Current CNNs excel at extracting intricate textures but often struggle with edge detection. Edge-related information, though present, goes unnoticed in traditional networks. To overcome this limitation, we propose an alternative edge-gated network that complements the existing texture extraction capability. In this approach, an auxiliary edge network, operating in parallel to the primary texture network, extracts edge cues. These two streams share a common code representation, obtained through a code-sharing layer. The combined code then passes through a code-fusion layer, integrating edge and texture information prior to output. We leverage a learned code to guide the edge network, ensuring it focuses on edge detection rather than texture. Notably, this edge network can be trained end-to-end, circumventing the need for separate edge-supervised training. We validated our method against multiple baseline models using public datasets for both natural and medical images, demonstrating its overall superiority.

MongoDB is a widely used NoSQL database for developing robust and transactionally
complex applications. However, verifying the transactional integrity of MongoDB-based
applications poses a challenge, primarily due to the absence of formal specifications
for its TDF (Transaction Protocol for Document-based File Systems) framework. To address
this issue, we created a novel approach to validate the transactional integrity of
MongoDB-based applications by mapping TDF's informal behavior into a mathematical
specification using Angluin's approach. We successfully applied this method to
validate the correctness of MongoDB's TDF implementation for nested documents.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric polynomials of Dyck paths with a bounce number of two via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of the coefficients in this expression, confirming a conjecture of Cho-Huh (2019) that the chromatic symmetric polynomials of these Dyck paths are $e$-positive.

From a bird's eye view, humans manage an array of complex tasks by relying on their sophisticated brain functions. Nevertheless, the exact mechanisms underlying these processes remain unclear even with advanced neuroscience knowledge. Hence, developing sophisticated, theoretically grounded models of human cognition seems challenging. This study takes an unconventional approach by introducing an unconventional model of human cognition, which we refer to as the "Executive Ability" framework. This model diverges from conventional machine learning concepts by not utilizing techniques such as optimization or the processing of raw data. Instead, it presents a unique resampling and relabeling strategy that leverages a contrastive value strategy guided by hindsight summarization. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of this model in achieving superior performance in various tasks, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques in multiple benchmarks, including the Santa Cruz Natural Language Task and the Visual Question Answering Task.

The accuracy of medical image analysis models, particularly those based on deep learning, can be vulnerable to biases inherent in their training data. This research proposes a novel framework that leverages explainable convolutional neural networks and measures the innate biases present in medical image collections without requiring corresponding clinical data. Specifically, it detects biases present in different organ regions of abdominal images by utilizing a visual backpropagation method that highlights regions of high activation intensity. By comparing the importance scores of each image region, it identifies and quantifies the biases present, and demonstrates its effectiveness through experiments conducted with multiple datasets. Furthermore, the proposed framework is versatile enough to accommodate multiple scoring metrics and can be applied to the evaluation of training datasets for medical image segmentation models, ultimately contributing to the development of more robust and generalized models.

In complex systems, where numerous elements interact with one another, it is frequently difficult to determine the underlying geometry and dynamic mechanisms responsible for the emergence of these phenomena. As a result, network models often rely on random or artificially designed configurations, which may deviate from true representations. In our study, we uncover the intricate architecture and dynamic processes underlying nanoscale assembly networks composed of triply interacting molecules. During spin reversal experiments, we observed both local and global thermal hysteresis in these networks, which couldn't be fully captured by existing models. By correlating microscale dynamics with macroscopic behavior, we identified critical events that lead to the formation of bistable networks and explain their dynamic histories. Moreover, we developed a new method to reconstruct temporal network geometry and dynamics from experimental data, allowing us to visualize the evolving assembly configuration and predict its behavior. This approach has broad implications for studying the intricate geometry and dynamics of complex systems revealed by experimental data.

The solar breeze, a flow of gas generated by the sun, creates various patterns in the corona, particularly in regions near solar equinoxes. Understanding this phenomenon is crucial for modeling gas flows in the inner solar system. As the solar breeze approaches the probe's location, its speed and temperature patterns are affected by the presence of shocks formed by interactions with the solar magnetic field. Due to the curved and changing field lines, measurements of certain plasma components are delayed, affecting observations of the solar breeze. From data collected during close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, we found that the speed of the solar breeze varies between 600 and 800 kilometers per second, with an average temperature of around 1.6 million degrees Kelvin. The composition of the solar breeze also changes depending on the distance to the sun, with the abundance of certain elements increasing or decreasing at different points. The results of these findings can be used to create more accurate models of the solar breeze and its effects on the solar system.

Speech emotion recognition enables robots to interact with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, achieving high accuracy rates across various speech data sets remains a challenge due to the inherent complexities in speech spectra. The problem is compounded by the fact that access to labeled training data is often restricted for many available datasets. We tackle these difficulties by designing a speech emotion recognition system based on transfer learning and adapted from deep reinforcement learning models. The proposed approach involves training a base model using data sets that are readily available, then adapting this model to new domains using the F-score reward function in a reinforcement learning framework. The results from our experiments indicate that the proposed approach yields superior performance when compared to non-domain adapted techniques, and is particularly effective in scenarios where data sets are heavily imbalanced.

We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high-pressure and we report that it exhibits ferrimagnetic properties similar to its isoelectronic counterpart, Bi$_2$CuO$_2$FeTiO$_5$, but with a significantly altered response to increased pressure. 

While Bi$_2$CuO$_2$FeTiO$_5$ exhibits a direct ferrimagnetic order that remains unaffected by high pressure, Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ undergoes a pressure-induced metamagnetic transition from a ferrimagnetic to a ferromagnetic order at 9 GPa. 

Additionally, we observe a distinct shift in the nuclear forward scattering signal from Bi and O atoms, indicating a change in the Bi anti-ferrimagnetic arrangement within the $c$-plane at 9 GPa, corresponding to the observed metamagnetic transition. 

Conversely, the magnetic arrangement along the c-axis remains unaltered at both 0 and 9 GPa. 

Furthermore, we measure an increase in the magnetic moment at 9 GPa, post-metamagnetic transition, and attribute this to a reduction in the anti-ferromagnetic interaction between Bi$^{3+}$ ions. 

Our findings are also consistent with the pressure-induced decrease in the bandwidth of the Bi $6s$

The concept of shortest paths has been widely adapted across various fields through the application of dynamic programming. Initially developed to resolve complex problems by breaking them down into more manageable sub-problems, it has now become a fundamental technique in network optimization. The traditional shortest path method can be either discrete, like A* search, or continuous, like steepest descent, depending on the nature of the problem at hand. Combining the two can be challenging due to the occurrence of singularities, extra computations, or approximation errors. A new approach has been developed to unify discrete and continuous shortest path methods by introducing a tolerable error limit, which can be set to zero, for practical applications such as free-flight path optimization. The unification approach uses the same underlying network flow algorithm, cutting plane algorithm, and a robust discrete-continuous network solver, allowing the error limit to be set to zero. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the unified approach by comparing it to traditional methods and applying it to a free-flight path optimization problem.

Researchers have observed that the internal structure of galaxy clusters features a cavity at their centers, which is believed to result from massive black holes active in the past. This cavity, likely formed by a powerful jet that emptied the cluster's interior, presents a complex shock front that has been the subject of interest for many years. The cavity's boundary is thought to be defined by a circular ring that shocks the surrounding gas as it expands. The issue with modeling this phenomenon using weak shock dynamics became apparent when scientists attempted to explain why the temperature of the gas on the cavity's boundary was not as high as expected. The project presented a new approach by modifying the standard adiabatic shock equation to account for the cavity's enclosed volume, which significantly raised the temperature of the gas at the boundary to around 10 keV. The new model also predicted that the temperature would drop to around 5 keV on the side of the shock wave facing the massive black hole. The findings of this research were validated by analyzing data from Chandra observations and suggested that the temperature drop could be attributed to a slow shock wave caused by the cluster's collapse. The project also revealed that the new approach can explain how the energy generated by a massive black hole is retained within the cluster.

A recent paper formulates a criterion for distinguishing discrete and semi-discrete short-systems in terms of a modified eigenvalue problem. Building on this, an extended class of generalized Hermite polynomials is defined to solve specific cases of these short-systems. These polynomials display key properties, including recurrence relations and non-standard orthogonality conditions, which are derived from the combinatorial framework of type-AA' Dynkin diagrams. Their explicit expressions are used to compute boundary values of conformal block operators, linking them to the semi-discrete Hirota equations. For graded Algebras U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2) and its dual, the discrete short-systems are solved by an inner product preserving transformation of the generalized Hermite polynomials. These polynomials are also shown to represent monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potentials, whose eigenvalues are given by the Casimir invariant.

The continuous changes in a tape's uncoiling dynamics are often accompanied by a persistent crackling noise, which appears random at first glance. However, our research reveals that beneath this seemingly chaotic sound lies a highly structured pattern. Using a high-speed camera and a sensitive microphone, we investigated the relationship between the tape's movement and the crackling noise. Our findings show that the noise is actually synchronized with the tape's spiral pattern. In particular, we discovered a specific 'fingerprint' of frequencies associated with the bacterial spiral pattern. Through mathematical modeling, we connected the tape's movement to the resulting sound. Our model highlights the importance of the tape's curvature in generating the characteristic frequencies observed in the sound spectrum. Furthermore, we identified a critical threshold for the tape's uncoiling velocity, which influences the spectrum's distribution. This interplay between the tape's geometry and motion determines the auditory experience as the tape unrolls.

In epitaxial samples, we generated planar JJ and SQUID devices using a combination of lithographic and etching techniques. By applying a consistent method for etching, we achieved a range of groove patterns from smooth to highly irregular. The phase-dynamics in these devices were influenced by the patterns formed during etching. A theoretical model was developed to simulate both local and long-range coupling between grains. By adjusting the grain size, we isolated the effect of the etching pattern on phase-dynamics. The theoretical predictions were validated through experimental measurements of DC and AC transport in these devices. The model revealed that in devices with highly irregular etching patterns, the critical current showed a stronger average-overlap dependence, while the effect of long-range coupling on the critical current was more pronounced in devices with smaller grains. The model also explained the observed ratio of idle and shunted critical currents in SQUIDs in terms of the grain size. The idle current was found to be more sensitive to phase-fluctuations when the grain size was larger than the Josephson length. The model further predicted that in JJ and SQUIDs with strongly coupled grains, the mean-overlap dependence of the critical current could be influenced by the presence of local-phase-fluctuations. The effect of long-range coupling on the critical current was found to be more pronounced when the grain size was smaller than the Josephson length. The model also explained the observed ratio of idle and shunted critical currents in SQUIDs in terms

We suggest a non-abelian generalization of the ether-like term that appears in the Dirac equation, and demonstrate its consistency with the principles of quantum field theory. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this modified ether term on the thermal equilibrium state of a quantum system, assuming that the temperature difference between two regions is significant enough that vacuum states cannot reach a common equilibrium.

This research develops a novel approach to modeling the complex dynamics of option collateral costs under constant delta hedging strategies.  A key aspect of this approach is identifying the relationship between option values, delta hedging costs, and the specific SABR model parameters.  This relationship takes the form of an explicit equation, which can be numerically solved using the method of stochastic alpha-beta-gamma (SABG) approximation.  By leveraging this relationship, a specific case can be examined in which delta hedging costs are directly subtracted from option payoffs.  A notable outcome of this research is the derivation of an analytical formula for the discounted option value, subject to delta hedging costs, under the SABR model.  This research has significant implications for both central clearing houses and systemic risk regulators, as it provides a precise mathematical formula for modeling the dynamics of option collateral costs.  A key benefit of this approach is the use of a consistent set of parameter values, as opposed to the current practice of employing various static approximations.  The accuracy of this model has been verified against a significant dataset of 100,000 Monte Carlo simulations.

This research addresses the long-term goal of creating a comprehensive framework for modeling materials with variable conductivity within mathematical homogenization theory. By parabolically replacing highly conductive inclusions with small sized holes, we first prove a key theorem that approximately maps the given equation to a simpler diffusion type equation. Next, we demonstrate that under this new representation, the original equation and its parabolic approximation have similar behavior over time. Additionally, we show that both the original and the new equations exhibit the same long-term average behavior. This discovery confirms a key conjecture made by the authors in their previous paper.

We undertook a statistical investigation into large, luminous elliptical galaxies and their occurrence of tidal features. Using data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program, we examined a sample of 3029 galaxies and found tidal features in 11%, affecting 21% of galaxies with absolute blue magnitudes less than -20.5. Features were generally circular and measured 11 kpc in size. In the field, we found a merger rate of 0.4 mergers per 10^9 years among early-type galaxies with the brightest central light. This was lower than estimated in a prior study, possibly due to differences in galaxy selection or the larger area covered in our analysis. A correlation existed between the fraction of light from a companion star and the mass ratio of the merger, with a threshold at 0.1. A more substantial proportion of low-mass ratio mergers occurred in the field, whereas equal-mass mergers prevailed in galaxy clusters. In the field, we found that one-quarter of large early-type galaxies had undergone low-mass ratio mergers, and three-quarters of these events occurred more than a billion years ago. A similar proportion of galaxy clusters consisted of galaxies that had undergone high-mass ratio mergers within the past billion years.

A social mobility theory suggests that children's social status is determined by a random element and their parent's social status. If social advancement is reinforced, the children of high-status households have a greater chance of achieving a higher status than those from low-status households. The model proposed exhibits dynamic behavior, and our analysis reveals that expectations are consistent with a stationary distribution that is normal, with a specific mean and variance. The variance of the distribution increases as the model transitions from a regime in which expectations are consistent with a normal distribution that is bimodal to a regime in which the distribution of social status is normal and monomodal. The variance also displays an irregular periodic increase as the model switches between regimes. The number of distinct variances that the distribution can exhibit is dependent on the level of social advancement and cannot be predicted by theoretical analysis. The findings support the hypothesis that increasing social advancement can result in a decline in the variance of social status.

I represent the Power Laser Facility, where I generated 90 W of power at a 10 kHz repetition rate and an 800 nm wavelength within a 100 ns pulse duration. However, this level of performance came with an 8 dB loss, primarily attributed to unoptimized amplifier operation. A more efficient configuration was then implemented to achieve 93 W of power at a 10 kHz rate, with a 100 ns pulse length and 800 nm wavelength. This new setup cut energy per pulse by half and significantly reduced the risk of damage, enabling better heat management and raising the possible power output to over 90 W. An amplifier design was subsequently identified that could produce 105 W of power at a 10 kHz rate, with a 100 ns pulse length and 800 nm wavelength. Building upon this design, I explored various options to further increase power output, including the use of multiple emitter bars and different pump configurations, which could potentially yield over 120 W of power at a 10 kHz rate, with a 100 ns pulse length and 800 nm wavelength.

We maintain an $\ell_p$ space with a specific dimension, ensuring that no more than an $\varepsilon$ fraction of its elements contain a particular vector of an specific length. Assuming this condition holds for some dimension $m$, we determine that there is an equivalent condition which states that no more than an $\varepsilon$ fraction of $m$-dimensional $\ell_p$ spaces contain the unit vector. This implies that $m$ is greater than $(\varepsilon' m)^{1/p} |E|^{p-1}$, with $\varepsilon' = \varepsilon'(\delta)$, for all $m \geq (1/\varepsilon')'^{-1}$, in the case when $1 < p < \infty$ and $m$ is greater than $(\varepsilon' m)^{1/2} |E|^{1-\frac{1}{p}}$ with $\varepsilon' = \varepsilon'(\delta)$, for all $m \geq (1/\varepsilon')'^{-1}$, in the case when $p < 1$.
